title: Better, Saner Homework Tips, Pt 2: Make It a Good Experience for Students
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: In the second installment, Stuart turns from the teacher's workload to the student's experience of homework. His argument is that good homework rests on purpose, proportion, and teaching: students should always know the point, the load should respect grade-level time limits, and every academic and behavioral move should be taught explicitly. He draws on Marzano and Pickering's rule of thumb of ten minutes times grade level, and on his own practice of having students reflect on where and when they do homework. A recurring thread is credibility, since assigning work he cannot justify risks misleading students and eroding trust. He closes by reframing homework as an act of respect toward adolescents, adjusted for younger children like his second-grade daughter.
points: Homework builds an academic identity, the belief that people like me do homework, so abstaining from it leaves secondary students unprepared for post-secondary expectations.
Stuart says that if he cannot link an assignment to long-term flourishing, the honest move is to question it in PLCs or department meetings rather than oversell it to students.
The Marzano and Pickering rule of grade level times ten gives a per-night ceiling, which for ninth graders with six teachers leaves him roughly fifteen minutes.
Both the academic side (reading to understand, making flashcards) and the behavioral side (when and where to work) of homework must be taught, checked, and retaught.
Presenting homework as respect works for adolescents, who crave being taken seriously, but must be reframed as opportunity for young children.
quotes: Motivationally, it gives them a chance to build an academic identity — to cultivate through experience the belief that “people like me do homework.” If we don't ever give homework, we don't ever give our students the chance to learn to think this way, to feel as though they can belong in settings where homework is a norm.

It's important to warn here that when we assign homework that we can't link to long-term flourishing, that we can't give great rationale for, then we're wiser to discuss this work's validity in PLCs or department meetings than we are to laud its greatness to our students. Teacher credibility is a fragile thing, and misleading students is the kind of behavior that undermines it.

take the students' grade level, multiply that by 10, and there you have the total number of minutes of homework that students should have on a given school night. For my ninth graders, this means 90 total minutes, and since I'm only one of their six teachers each day, I get about 15 minutes per night.

The academic side of a homework assignment must be clearly taught, checked, retaught as needed, and monitored afterward. I wrote about this a bit in the aforementioned homework post, but it merits repeating. Every move involved in a given homework assignment needs to be taught, checked, retaught as needed, and refreshed from time to time afterward.

After this warm-up, we Think-Pair-Share and then spend a few moments discussing (via a mini-pop-up or a Conversation Challenge) the last bullet point. My goal is to guide students to start understanding their homework habits and how they might improve them.

Were I to refrain from giving you purposeful homework,” I explain to my students, “I would not be taking you seriously.” Homework, in my classroom, is a sign of my respect for my students. This is an important note, as so much of my credibility in their eyes comes from whether or not they sense that I take them seriously.
